lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
A gate is often the first thing a visitor sees at a home or business. In many African communities, a well-built metal gate signals security, status, and craftsmanship. For you as an ornamental ironworker, gate construction is a core skill that can earn steady income. Unlike a simple fence, a gate must open and close smoothly, withstand daily use, and look good. This module will teach you how to design and build gates that are strong, safe, and attractive.

Why focus on gates? Because every compound, shop, and school needs at least one. In cities like Lagos, Nairobi, or Accra, demand for custom gates is high. A basic single swing gate can sell for 50,000 to 150,000 Naira (or equivalent) depending on size and design. With the right skills, you can produce 2â3 gates per month and build a reputation. But poor work leads to sagging hinges, rust, and unhappy customers. So learn it right.

This module covers six lessons: introduction, tools and materials, step-by-step method, common mistakes, safety, and a practical exercise. You will learn to measure, cut, weld, and finish a gate from start to finish. We assume you have basic welding and metalworking skills, but even if you are new, follow along carefully. By the end, you will be able to design a simple single swing gate and build it to last.

Remember: a gate is not just a barrier; it is a product you sell. Quality work brings referrals. Take pride in every joint and every weld. Let's get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To build a gate, you need the right tools and materials. Without them, you will waste time and produce weak work. Here is a practical list for a basic single swing gate, 3 feet wide and 6 feet tall.

Tools: A welding machine (arc welder, 200â250 amps) with electrodes (2.5mm or 3.2mm, e.g., E6013). An angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs. A tape measure (5m), try square, spirit level, and chalk or marker. A hacksaw for small cuts. A drill with metal bits for hinges. A hammer, chisel, and files. Clamps to hold pieces. Safety gear: welding helmet, gloves, apron, boots, and goggles.

Materials: Mild steel square tubes (e.g., 25mm x 25mm x 2mm) for the frame. Flat bars (25mm x 5mm) for decorative scrolls or hinges. Round bars (10mm or 12mm) for pickets. Hinges (weld-on or bolt-on, 2â3 per gate). A latch or lock. Primer and paint (anti-rust). Concrete mix for posts (if installing).

Where to buy: In most African cities, visit a steel merchant or scrap market. For example, in Kano, Nigeria, the Sabon Gari market has steel. In Nairobi, check Industrial Area. Buy from a trusted supplier to avoid weak steel. Always measure twice and cut once. Keep a small notebook to record your cut list. Pre-cut all pieces before welding to save time. With these tools and materials, you are ready to build.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps to build a simple single swing gate. We assume a finished size of 3ft wide x 6ft tall.

Step 1: Design and measure. Sketch your gate. Decide on frame, pickets, and decoration. Measure the opening where the gate will hang. Allow 1/2 inch clearance on each side and bottom for movement. So if opening is 37 inches wide, gate should be 36 inches wide. Height: 72 inches.

Step 2: Cut pieces. For the frame, cut two vertical tubes 72 inches long, and two horizontal tubes 36 inches long. For pickets, cut round bars 60 inches long (leaving space for top and bottom rails). You need about 7 pickets spaced 4 inches apart. Cut flat bars for scrolls if desired.

Step 3: Build the frame. Lay the tubes on a flat surface (a welding table or concrete floor). Use clamps to hold the rectangle square. Check with a try square. Weld the corners. Grind smooth.

Step 4: Add pickets. Mark positions on the top and bottom rails. Tack weld each picket in place. Check spacing and vertical alignment. Then weld fully.

Step 5: Attach hinges and latch. Weld one hinge leaf to the gate frame and the other to the post. For a 3ft gate, use two hinges (top and bottom). For heavier gates, use three. Weld a latch or lock box on the opposite side.

Step 6: Finish. Grind all welds. Clean with a wire brush. Apply primer, then two coats of paint. Let dry.

Step 7: Install. Set posts in concrete, ensuring they are plumb. Hang the gate, check swing. Adjust if needed. Lubricate hinges. Your gate is ready.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Even experienced welders make mistakes. Here are common ones and how to fix them.

Mistake 1: Gate not square. If the frame is not square, the gate will not close properly. Fix: Always check diagonals. Measure from top-left to bottom-right and top-right to bottom-left. They must be equal. If not, adjust before welding.

Mistake 2: Weak welds. Poor penetration causes cracks. Fix: Use correct amperage (e.g., 90â120 amps for 2.5mm electrode). Clean metal before welding. Practice on scrap.

Mistake 3: Hinges placed wrong. If hinges are too far apart or misaligned, gate will sag. Fix: Align hinges perfectly. Use a level. For a 6ft gate, top hinge about 6 inches from top, bottom hinge about 6 inches from bottom. Weld securely.

Mistake 4: No allowance for expansion. Metal expands in heat. If gate fits too tight, it will jam. Fix: Leave 1/4 to 1/2 inch gap around gate.

Mistake 5: Poor rust protection. Bare steel rusts quickly, especially in humid or coastal areas. Fix: Apply primer and at least two coats of outdoor paint. Use galvanized steel if budget allows.

Mistake 6: Ignoring safety. Welding without helmet or gloves causes injury. Fix: Always wear PPE. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby.

Mistake 7: Not testing. Always test gate swing before final installation. Fix: Hang gate temporarily, open and close. Adjust as needed. Learn from each mistake. A good gate is a series of small correct decisions.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is not optional. As an ornamental ironworker, you face hazards: burns, eye damage, cuts, and electrical shock. Follow these rules to stay safe and produce quality work.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Always wear a welding helmet with proper shade (shade 10 for arc welding). Use leather gloves, apron, and steel-toe boots. Wear safety glasses when grinding or cutting. Use earplugs if noise is loud. Never weld in shorts or open shoes.

Workshop safety: Keep your work area clean. Remove flammable materials. Ensure good ventilationâwelding fumes are toxic. Use a welding screen to protect others. Check electrical cords for damage. Ground your welder properly. Keep a fire extinguisher and first aid kit nearby.

Best practices: Plan your work. Measure twice, cut once. Use jigs or clamps for repeatability. Keep your tools sharp and maintained. Weld on a flat, fireproof surface. Grind welds smooth for a professional finish. Paint immediately after cleaning to prevent rust.

Ergonomics: Lift with your legs, not your back. Use a trolley for heavy steel. Take breaks to avoid fatigue.

Environmental care: Dispose of metal scraps responsibly. Recycle where possible. Avoid breathing zinc fumes from galvanized steelâwear a respirator.

By following these practices, you protect yourself and your customers. A safe worker is a productive worker. Remember, no gate is worth an injury.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to build a gate. This exercise will guide you through making a small single swing gate, 2 feet wide x 4 feet tall. Use scrap or new steel.

Materials: 20mm square tubes for frame (2 pieces 48 inches, 2 pieces 24 inches). 10mm round bars for pickets (5 pieces 36 inches). 2 hinges, 1 latch. Primer and paint.

Tools: Welder, grinder, tape measure, square, clamps, drill, safety gear.

Steps:
1. Cut all pieces to length. Clean ends.
2. Lay frame tubes on flat surface. Clamp square. Check diagonals. Weld corners.
3. Mark picket positions on top and bottom rails: space evenly, about 4 inches apart. Tack weld pickets. Check vertical. Weld fully.
4. Grind welds smooth.
5. Attach hinges to one side: top hinge 4 inches from top, bottom hinge 4 inches from bottom. Weld. Attach latch on other side.
6. Clean with wire brush. Apply primer, then two coats of paint. Let dry.
7. Install on a post (you can use a wooden post for practice). Check swing.

Evaluation: Does gate open and close smoothly? Are welds strong? Is it square? Is paint even? Take a photo for your portfolio.

Time: 4â6 hours. Cost: about 5,000â10,000 Naira (or equivalent) for materials. This small gate teaches all key skills. Repeat until confident. Then move to larger gates.

quiz.q: What is the main reason gate construction is important for an ornamental ironworker?
options: A) It is easy to do
B) It is a core skill that can earn steady income
D) It is only for decoration
quiz.explanation: Gate construction is a core skill that is in high demand and can generate income.

quiz.q: What is a typical price range for a basic single swing gate in African cities?
quiz.explanation: A basic single swing gate can sell for 50,000 to 150,000 Naira depending on size and design.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a tool needed for gate construction?
quiz.explanation: A wood saw is not typically used for metal gate construction; a hacksaw or angle grinder is used instead.

quiz.q: What type of electrode is commonly used for arc welding gates?
quiz.explanation: E6013 is a common general-purpose electrode for arc welding mild steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance around a gate to allow for expansion?
quiz.explanation: A gap of 1/4 to 1/2 inch allows for metal expansion and smooth operation.

quiz.q: When building a gate frame, how do you ensure it is square?
options: C) By using a spirit level only
quiz.explanation: Measuring diagonals ensures the frame is square; they must be equal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of pickets in a gate?
options: B) To provide security and decoration
D) To make it easier to weld
quiz.explanation: Pickets are vertical bars that add security and aesthetic appeal.

quiz.q: How many hinges are recommended for a 3ft wide gate?
quiz.explanation: Two hinges (top and bottom) are sufficient for a 3ft gate; heavier gates may need three.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding to prevent weak welds?
quiz.explanation: Clean metal ensures good weld penetration and strength.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that causes a gate to sag?
quiz.explanation: Misaligned or poorly placed hinges cause the gate to sag.

quiz.q: How can you protect a gate from rust?
quiz.explanation: Primer and paint provide a protective barrier against rust.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a gate?
quiz.explanation: Designing and measuring ensures you have a plan and correct dimensions.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential for welding?
quiz.explanation: A welding helmet protects eyes and face from sparks and UV radiation.

quiz.q: Why is good ventilation important when welding?
options: A) To keep the metal cool
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes can be toxic; good ventilation removes them.

quiz.q: What should you do before final installation of a gate?
quiz.explanation: Testing the swing ensures it opens and closes properly before final fixing.

quiz.q: What is a jig used for?
quiz.explanation: A jig holds pieces in place for consistent, repeatable work.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a welding helmet for arc welding?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10 is standard for arc welding to protect against bright light.

quiz.q: What should you do with metal scraps?
quiz.explanation: Recycling metal scraps is environmentally responsible.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a latch on a gate?
quiz.explanation: A latch or lock keeps the gate closed and secure.

quiz.q: How can you avoid back injury when lifting steel?
quiz.explanation: Lifting with your legs reduces strain on your back.

quiz.q: What is the typical amperage range for welding 2.5mm electrode?
quiz.explanation: 90â120 amps is suitable for 2.5mm electrodes on mild steel.

quiz.q: Why should you grind welds smooth?
quiz.explanation: Grinding welds smooth improves appearance and removes sharp edges.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if a gate does not close properly?
options: B) Check if it is square
quiz.explanation: Checking squareness helps identify alignment issues.

quiz.q: What is a good spacing for pickets on a gate?
quiz.explanation: 4 inches is a common spacing that balances security and visibility.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding galvanized steel?
quiz.explanation: Zinc fumes are toxic; remove coating or use a respirator.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a primer?
quiz.explanation: Primer provides a protective base coat that prevents rust.

quiz.q: How many coats of paint are recommended for a gate?
quiz.explanation: Two coats of paint provide good coverage and protection.

quiz.q: What is the best surface for welding a gate frame?
quiz.explanation: A flat, fireproof surface like concrete ensures a level frame.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a minor burn?
quiz.explanation: Cooling a burn with water reduces damage and pain.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a fire extinguisher nearby?
options: A) To put out welding fires
quiz.explanation: Welding can cause fires; a fire extinguisher is essential for safety.
